claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is single-phase BCC.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has high density and insufficient room-temperature ductility.
Adding a minor amount of Si to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce precipitation or spinodal decomposition.
Si addition will produce a C15 Laves phase in the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr matrix.
The proposed C15 phase will have an Hf-Mo-Si or similar composition.
The C15 Laves phase will form a continuous or semi-continuous reticulated network within the BCC matrix.
A secondary C15 phase can coexist with a BCC refractory-alloy matrix.
The reticulated Laves-phase network will act as a physical barrier to crack propagation.
The network will force cracks to deflect or branch.
Ductile BCC matrix ligaments will bridge cracks around the Laves-phase network.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix in another RHEA is associated with high yield strength but brittle room-temperature compressive failure.
A weakly ordered single-phase BCC state can be much more ductile than a continuous B2-matrix state.
The Si-modified alloy will have yield strength comparable to or higher than the baseline because of precipitation hardening.
The reticulated network will significantly increase room-temperature compressive strain to failure relative to the baseline.
Si addition and formation of the Laves phase will cause a marginal increase in alloy density.
Discrete isolated secondary-phase particles will not provide the proposed ductility improvement.
A continuous brittle secondary-phase matrix will suppress the proposed ductility improvement.
The proposed effect is limited to room-temperature compression under conditions where the BCC matrix remains ductile.
Arc melting followed by homogenization and controlled cooling or annealing can facilitate the proposed phase separation.
Correlating secondary-phase morphology and crack paths with room-temperature compression behavior across Si concentrations can test the proposed phase-structure mechanism.
